# Methods

**34 harmonization methods** are registered. Five more are deliberately absent; see the bottom of this page for each one's reason.

`combobatch list-methods` prints this same table from the same registry, and `--available-only` narrows it to what your environment can actually run.

## Citations and notes

**`01_raw`** — No correction; the baseline every metric is read against.

**`02_median_scaling`** — Per-batch median centring.

**`07_pycombat`** — Behdenna et al. 2023, BMC Bioinformatics (pyComBat).

**`08_inmoose_combatseq`** — Zhang et al. 2020, NAR Genom Bioinform (ComBat-seq), via InMoose.

**`11_harmony`** — Korsunsky et al. 2019, Nat Methods.

**`12_scanorama`** — Hie et al. 2019, Nat Biotechnol.

**`13_fsmvn`** — Feature-specific mean-variance normalization.

**`15_fsqn_py`** — Franks et al. 2018, Biostatistics (FSQN), Python implementation.

**`17_quantile`** — Bolstad et al. 2003, Bioinformatics.

**`18_rank`** — Fractional rank transform; platform-independent by construction.

**`25_angel`** — Angel et al. 2020, PLOS Comput Biol.
  Reduces the gene space rather than correcting values, so its metrics are not directly comparable with the other methods.

**`26_xpn`** — Shabalin et al. 2008, Bioinformatics (XPN).

**`30_recombat`** — Adossa et al. 2021 (reComBat).

**`03_limma`** — Ritchie et al. 2015, NAR (limma::removeBatchEffect).

**`04_sva`** — Leek & Storey 2012, Bioinformatics (SVA).

**`05_combat`** — Johnson et al. 2007, Biostatistics (ComBat).

**`06_combat_seq`** — Zhang et al. 2020, NAR Genom Bioinform (ComBat-seq).

**`09_ruv`** — Risso et al. 2014, Nat Biotechnol (RUVg).

**`10_mnn`** — Haghverdi et al. 2018, Nat Biotechnol (fastMNN).

**`14_qsmooth`** — Hicks et al. 2018, Biostatistics (qsmooth).

**`22_tmm`** — Robinson & Oshlack 2010, Genome Biol (TMM via edgeR).

**`23_vst`** — Love et al. 2014, Genome Biol (DESeq2 VST).

**`16_fsqn_r`** — Franks et al. 2018, Biostatistics (FSQN R package).

**`19_tdm`** — Thompson et al. 2016, BMC Bioinformatics (TDM).

**`20_shambhala`** — Borisov et al. 2021, Bioinformatics (Shambhala2); CuBlock.
  Replaces the donor's Shambhala2 R package with the containerized pure-Python + Octave implementation, so results are not bit-identical to the published benchmark rows. Samples are harmonized independently, so no batch column is used. Output genes are the input's intersection with P and Q.

**`21_harmonizr`** — Voss et al. 2022, Bioinformatics (HarmonizR).

**`27_dwd`** — Qing & Marron 2018 (DWDLargeR).

**`28_npn`** — Liu et al. 2009, JMLR (nonparanormal), via huge.

**`29_combat_ref`** — M-ComBat: ComBat anchored to a reference batch (sva).

**`31_ruv3prps`** — Molania et al. 2022, NAR (RUV-III-PRPS).

**`33_amdbnorm`** — AMDBNorm (PMID 34958674), on DBNorm.

**`34_arsyn`** — Nueda et al. 2012, Bioinformatics (ARSyN), via NOISeq.

**`37_fabatch`** — Hornung et al. 2016, BMC Bioinformatics (FAbatch), via bapred.
  bapred::fabatch structurally requires a two-level target, so this method skips honestly on datasets whose target column has any other number of levels.

**`38_harman`** — Oytam et al. 2016, BMC Bioinformatics (Harman).

## Three rules that apply across methods

**The RNA-seq-only guard.** Methods marked *RNA-seq only* model counts and are meaningless on microarray intensities. Rather than producing plausible nonsense, they raise `NotImplementedError` when the batch column contains a non-RNA-seq batch — an honest skip, recorded as such in the sidecar.

**Reference-batch resolution.** Methods marked *uses reference batch* map every batch onto one target. When `target_group` is not given it resolves to **the largest batch in the data**, never to a hardcoded name. Set `--reference-batch` to choose a different target space.

**Harshness** is how aggressively a method reshapes the matrix: `low` methods adjust location and scale, `high` methods reshape the distribution itself. It travels into every sidecar so a result can be read alongside how much violence was done to get it.

## `20_shambhala` is a re-implementation

The original Shambhala is an R package that was not usable here. `20_shambhala` is the vendored pure-Python plus Octave implementation, which follows the same algorithm but is not bit-identical to the R original. Numbers from it should not be compared directly against published Shambhala results without saying so.

Two constraints it does not share with any other method: input must be **raw, not log-scale** (it applies its own `log2(x+1)` and has no scale detection), and its parallelism **multiplies** with the dispatcher's — total Octave processes are outer workers times its own `n_workers`.

## Deliberately absent (5)

These keys existed upstream and are not registered here. The numbering keeps its gaps so that a key always means the same method it always meant.

| Key | Why |
|---|---|
| `24_peer_k10` | PEER is unavailable for R 4.5 (not on CRAN, Bioconductor or GitHub) |
| `32_deepmnn` | scRNA-seq only; needs AnnData + HVG + PCA, not applicable to bulk |
| `35_dasc` | returns cluster assignments, not a corrected expression matrix |
| `36_explobatch` | hard dependency fMM had its GitHub repository deleted |
| `39_procrustes` | licence-restricted: BostonGene proprietary, non-commercial research use only, and forbids altering copyright notices - incompatible with an MIT tool |

`39_procrustes` deserves the longest note. It is not a technical exclusion: the implementation works. It is BostonGene proprietary, licensed for non-commercial research only, and its licence forbids altering copyright notices — all three of which are incompatible with an MIT-licensed public tool. No clone, no `sys.path` insertion, no optional dependency: it is absent from the image entirely.
